title: Clinical Documentation from Doctor Dictation
summary: Doctors dictate in English or Hinglish after a consultation, round or procedure, and the system drafts a structured note or prescription in your EMR template for the doctor to check and sign.

seo.title: Clinical Notes from Doctor Dictation with AI | VipraTech
seo.description: Dictation-to-note for OPD, ward and OT documentation, tuned for Indian English, Hinglish and drug names, with formulary checks and doctor sign-off.

designed_for: Head of Medical Transcription or MRD

problem.intro: Doctors in busy OPDs and wards either type notes between patients, write them by hand or leave them for later. Medical transcription takes time and still needs correcting. Indian doctors often dictate in English mixed with Hindi, with drug brand names and abbreviations that general speech tools get wrong.

pain_points.title: Typing time in short consultations
pain_points.detail: Doctors split attention between the patient and the screen, or write brief notes that miss detail.

pain_points.title: Vocabulary errors
pain_points.detail: Generic speech tools mangle drug brands, doses, abbreviations and anatomical terms.

pain_points.title: Unstructured output
pain_points.detail: Free-text dictation does not fill the EMR fields that billing, audits and other teams rely on.

pain_points.title: Sound-alike drug risk
pain_points.detail: Drug names that sound similar can be transcribed wrongly, which is a patient safety issue if nobody catches it.

solution.overview: We build a dictation-to-note system for OPD, ward and OT documentation. The doctor dictates on a phone, tablet or desktop microphone, in English or Hinglish, after the consultation or procedure. Speech recognition tuned to your specialties, formulary and common brand names produces a transcript, and an LLM organises it into your EMR template: complaints, history, examination, the doctor's stated assessment, plan and prescription lines. It uses only what the doctor said. Drug names are checked against your formulary, and unrecognised or sound-alike names, missing doses and unusual frequencies are highlighted. The doctor reviews the draft beside the audio, corrects it and signs.
capabilities: Speech recognition tuned for Indian English, Hinglish, drug brands and specialty vocabulary
Structuring into OPD, ward round, operative note and prescription templates
Formulary check that highlights unrecognised or sound-alike drug names and missing doses
Side-by-side review with transcript, audio playback and highlighted uncertain words
Write-back of signed notes and prescriptions to the EMR

workflow.title: Dictate
workflow.detail: The doctor records a dictation on a mobile app or desktop after the consultation, round or procedure, linked to the patient's UHID.

workflow.title: Transcribe
workflow.detail: Specialty-tuned speech recognition converts the audio to text and marks uncertain words.

workflow.title: Structure into the template
workflow.detail: An LLM places the content into the right template sections without adding information.

workflow.title: Check drugs and gaps
workflow.detail: Prescription lines are checked against the formulary, and sound-alike names, missing doses and empty mandatory sections are highlighted.

workflow.title: Doctor review and sign
workflow.detail: The doctor reviews the draft with audio playback, corrects it and signs.

workflow.title: Write to the EMR
workflow.detail: The signed note and prescription are written to the EMR, and the audio is kept or deleted according to policy.

inputs: Patient context from the EMR, such as UHID and visit type
Specialty templates for OPD, ward and operative notes
Hospital formulary with brand and generic names
outputs: Structured draft note in the EMR template
Draft prescription lines with formulary flags
Highlighted uncertain words with audio links
Signed note and prescription in the EMR
Audit trail of draft, edits and signature
human_in_the_loop: The doctor reviews and signs every note and prescription. The system only structures what the doctor dictated; it does not suggest diagnoses, treatments or doses.
integrations: EMR or HIS (API, HL7 or FHIR)
Mobile device management for hospital devices
Existing transcription workflow where some departments keep it
guardrails: No content added beyond the dictation; empty sections stay empty
Sound-alike and unrecognised drug names always highlighted
Drafts cannot be printed or shared until signed
Audio encrypted and kept only as long as policy allows
Recording of consultations only with the patient's recorded consent
compliance_notes: Audio and notes are health data under the DPDP Act 2023; consent, access control and retention follow hospital policy.
For US deployments, designed to operate under HIPAA safeguards with a business associate agreement.
The doctor remains the author of the record and responsible for its clinical content.

pilot.scope: OPD notes and prescriptions for a small group of consultants in one or two specialties, run alongside their current documentation.
deliverables: Templates and vocabulary for the pilot specialties

what_we_measure.how: Word error rate on a reviewed sample, reported separately for drug names and clinical terms.
Changes made between the draft and the signed note.
Pharmacist or doctor review of whether each formulary flag was justified, and of any drug error that was not flagged.
Doctor-reported and app-measured time per note compared with their current method.

faqs.q: Does it understand Hinglish and Indian accents?
faqs.a: Yes. We tune recognition with your specialties' vocabulary and test it on dictations from your own doctors. The pilot reports accuracy per doctor and per term type.

faqs.q: Will it suggest diagnoses or medicines?
faqs.a: No. It structures what the doctor said. It flags drug names it cannot match to the formulary or that sound like another drug, but it never proposes a drug or dose.

faqs.q: Is patient audio sent outside the hospital?
faqs.a: Processing can run in your cloud account in an India region, or on hospital servers for the speech component. We agree the deployment model with your IT and data protection teams.

faqs.q: Can it replace our transcription team?
faqs.a: Many hospitals keep transcriptionists as reviewers for complex dictations such as operative notes. The pilot shows where doctors can self-review and where a second reviewer still adds value.
